1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: The patient is a 43-year-old woman with the chief complaint of "cough and sputum production for 8 months, dyspnea for more than 1 month." In approximately 8 months before Day 0, she developed paroxysmal cough without an obvious trigger, producing yellow thick sputum in a small amount, without fever, night sweats, chest tightness, or shortness of breath. After self-purchasing and taking anti-inflammatory medication, the symptoms improved somewhat. In approximately 3 months before Day 0, after an episode of catching a cold, her cough and sputum production worsened; the sputum became white and frothy, in a large amount, approximately 750 ml/d, occasionally blood-streaked, with intermittent fever, maximum temperature 38.5℃, without chills or rigors. At a local hospital, she was treated with piperacillin/sulbactam and levofloxacin for anti-infective therapy for 7 days. The fever and hemoptysis improved somewhat, but the cough and sputum production did not improve. In approximately 1 month before Day 0, the cough and sputum production worsened significantly, with yellow frothy sputum, approximately 1500 ml/d. At an outside hospital, she received 4-drug anti-TB treatment for 15 days without obvious improvement. Thereafter, the patient developed dyspnea, which gradually worsened, with cyanosis of the lips. The emergency department considered bacterial coinfection with fungal infection and treated her with latamoxef and fluconazole for 6 days, but her dyspnea did not improve. Since disease onset, bowel and bladder habits have been normal, and her weight decreased by 3 kg over the past month. Past history: usually healthy; no history of hepatitis B; no history of HIV or close contact exposure; no history of TB or close contact exposure. In approximately 28 months before Day 0, she underwent "hysterectomy, oophorectomy, and lymph node dissection" for "cervical cancer." No drug allergies. Personal history unremarkable. Physical examination: temperature 36.2℃, heart rate 112 beats/min, respiratory rate 36 breaths/min, blood pressure 109/70 mmHg. Chronically ill appearance, orthopnea, no palpable superficial lymphadenopathy. Cardiac and abdominal examinations showed no abnormalities, and no clubbing of the fingers/toes was seen. Trachea midline. Bilateral respiratory movements were symmetric. Coarse breath sounds were heard in both lungs, with a small amount of moist rales in both lower lungs. Laboratory tests: CBC: WBC 11.9×10^9/L, PLT 385×10^9/L, neutrophil percentage 66.1%, lymphocyte percentage 18.5%. Routine stool and urine tests + OB negative. Liver and kidney function: ALT 35 IU/L, Cr 68 μmol/L. D-dimer 0.89 mg/L, ESR 120 mm/h, T-SPOT positive (A: 6, B: 0). Quantitative PCT 0.05 ng/ml. Tests for syphilis, HIV, Mycoplasma, viral hepatitis, and virus- and parasite-related pathogens were all negative; TB antibody (-), PPD skin test (-), T-SPOT negative. Lung cancer panel: CYFRA 21-1 4.31, cytokeratin-19 8.73, neuron-specific enolase, squamous cell carcinoma antigen, and carcinoembryonic antigen were normal. Sputum Gram stain: large numbers of Gram-positive bacteria and relatively many Gram-negative bacteria. Bedside color Doppler ultrasound: bilateral pleural effusions, neither suitable for puncture localization. Chest CT (Day 0): diffuse bilateral pulmonary nodules, some with cavitation; consolidation in both lower lungs and the right upper lung: fungal infection highly possible, please correlate clinically; follow-up review after treatment is recommended. Multiple enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes, small left pleural effusion, small pericardial effusion.

differential_diagnoses.name: Invasive pulmonary fungal infection
supporting_evidence: Chest CT suggested: "Diffuse bilateral pulmonary nodules, some with cavitation; consolidation in both lower lungs and the right upper lung: fungal infection is highly likely; please correlate clinically; follow-up reexamination after treatment is recommended"
The disease course has been prolonged for 8 months, with recent progressive worsening, accompanied by dyspnea and cyanosis of the lips, consistent with severe pulmonary infection.
Intermittent fever, a 3 kg weight loss over nearly 1 month, and ESR 120 mm/h suggest a significant inflammatory or consumptive process.

After antibacterial treatment, fever and hemoptysis improved somewhat, but cough, sputum production, and dyspnea continued to progress, suggesting that routine bacterial infection cannot fully explain the condition.
Imaging shows some cavitation, consolidation, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and small pleural and pericardial effusions, findings that can be seen in invasive infection.
opposing_evidence: Previously generally healthy, with no history of AIDS; the first-stage information did not indicate a definite immunosuppressed state.
After 6 days of fluconazole treatment in the emergency department, dyspnea did not improve.
Sputum Gram stain showed numerous gram-positive bacteria and a relatively large number of gram-negative bacteria, suggesting possible coinfection or a greater likelihood of a bacterial pathogen.

Chest CT showed diffuse nodules in both lungs, some with cavitation, and multiple enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes, which can be seen in pulmonary tuberculosis.
ESR is significantly elevated at 120 mm/h, supporting the possibility of chronic granulomatous infection.
The Phase 1 text includes the information "T-SPOT positive (A: 6, B: 0)".
opposing_evidence: No history of TB or close contact exposure
TB antibody (-), PPD skin test (-)

differential_diagnoses.name: Invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma of the lung (formerly bronchioloalveolar carcinoma type)
supporting_evidence: Expectorating large amounts of foamy sputum with a progressive increase, approximately 750 ml/d to 1500 ml/d, representing marked bronchial hypersecretion and suggesting the possibility of a mucin-secreting tumor
After antibacterial treatment and anti-tuberculosis treatment, cough and sputum production did not improve significantly, suggesting a lesion that is not purely infectious.
Progressive dyspnea and weight loss, consistent with the possibility of malignancy

Chest CT shows diffuse bilateral pulmonary nodules and multilobar consolidation, which may be seen with aerogenous spread or diffuse intrapulmonary involvement of lung adenocarcinoma, especially the mucinous type.
In the five lung cancer markers, CYFRA21-1 4.31 and cytokeratin-19 8.73 were elevated, suggesting an increased likelihood of pulmonary malignancy.
opposing_evidence: Intermittent fever, markedly elevated ESR, and a large number of bacteria seen on Gram stain of sputum are more supportive of an infectious process or tumor with superimposed infection.
The CT report initially suggested a high likelihood of fungal infection.
The phase I information did not provide a clear description of a primary pulmonary space-occupying lesion or a typical mass.

differential_diagnoses.name: Necrotizing bacterial pneumonia / multiple lung abscesses
supporting_evidence: There is cough with yellow thick sputum, later progressing to a large amount of yellow foamy sputum, accompanied by intermittent fever and occasional blood-streaked sputum, consistent with manifestations of severe suppurative pulmonary infection.
Sputum Gram stain showed a large number of Gram-positive bacteria and a relatively large number of Gram-negative bacteria, supporting bacterial infection.
Complete blood count: WBC 11.9×10^9/L, suggesting an inflammatory response
CT showed diffuse bilateral pulmonary nodules, some with cavitation, and consolidation in both lower lungs and the right upper lung, which may be seen in necrotizing pneumonia or abscess formation

A small amount of moist rales could be heard in both lower lungs. Bedside color Doppler ultrasound showed bilateral pleural effusions, consistent with severe pulmonary infection with pleural effusions.
opposing_evidence: The disease course lasted 8 months, longer than that of typical acute bacterial pneumonia
After multiple antimicrobial treatments, cough, sputum production, and dyspnea still showed no significant improvement
PCT 0.05 ng/ml, not supportive of overt active severe bacterial infection
Multiple enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes and a small pericardial effusion suggest that other infectious or neoplastic diseases should be considered.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary metastases (postoperative pulmonary metastases from cervical cancer, with cavitation or secondary infection)
supporting_evidence: She previously underwent uterine, ovarian, and lymph node dissection surgery for "cervical cancer" in approximately 28 months before Day 0, with a history of malignancy.
Chest CT showed diffuse nodules in both lungs, compatible with the imaging appearance of hematogenous pulmonary metastases.
Accompanied by multiple enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes, a small pleural effusion, and pericardial effusion, suggesting the possibility of a neoplastic lesion
Weight loss of 3 kg over the past month, supporting the possibility of a wasting disease
opposing_evidence: Copious foamy sputum and intermittent fever are not typical initial manifestations of pulmonary metastases alone.
CT showed cavitation in some lesions and favored fungal infection; an infectious etiology was the primary consideration based on imaging.
Sputum Gram stain showed numerous bacteria, suggesting a concomitant or more likely infectious process.

differential_diagnoses.name: Nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary disease
supporting_evidence: Female, chronic cough and sputum production for 8 months, with gradual worsening recently, consistent with the chronic course seen in nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary disease
CT shows diffuse bilateral pulmonary nodules, some with cavitation and consolidation, an imaging pattern seen in mycobacterial infection.
Poor response to empiric antibacterial therapy, suggesting a possible non-common bacterial infection
Weight loss and elevated ESR support the possibility of chronic infectious disease.
opposing_evidence: Phase 1 information did not provide acid-fast staining, mycobacterial culture, or related microbiologic evidence.
A very large sputum volume reaching 1500 ml/d is not a typical feature of nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary disease.
Sputum Gram stain has already shown a large number of common bacteria, suggesting other pathogens more directly.
The phase 1 information did not provide clear contradictory evidence.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: CT-guided lung biopsy pathology result: (lung) well- to moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma, likely primary.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient is a 43-year-old woman with cough and sputum production for 8 months, with a recent marked increase in sputum volume to approximately 1500 ml/d and progressive dyspnea, accompanied by weight loss, lip cyanosis, and type I respiratory failure; the condition is severe and rapidly progressive. Previous chest CT showed diffuse bilateral pulmonary nodules, partial cavitation, consolidation in both lower lungs and the right upper lung, and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Infection such as fungal infection or TB was at one point highly suspected early on, but antibacterial, anti-TB, and empiric antifungal therapy all produced no significant improvement, and bronchoscopy showed only foamy secretions with no neoplasm seen, suggesting that the nature of the disease could not be determined by clinical findings and imaging alone. At this point, CT-guided direct sampling of the pulmonary parenchymal lesions is needed to address the key question of whether the diffuse pulmonary lesions represent infection, inflammation, or tumor, and if tumor, whether primary or metastatic. This examination can provide a histopathologic basis for definitive diagnosis, can exclude the persistently problematic infectious and non-neoplastic differential diagnoses, and can also provide the prerequisite for subsequent staging assessment, molecular testing, and treatment strategy selection.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Immunohistochemistry results: Napsin A (-), Ki67 (50%), TTF (-), MUC5AC (+), CA12-5 (-), EML-ALK (-), GATA3 (-);
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: Although percutaneous lung biopsy pathology suggested well- to moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma with a high likelihood of primary origin, the imaging findings in this case showed diffuse bilateral pulmonary nodules and consolidation, the clinical presentation was characterized by copious foamy sputum, and there was a prior history of postoperative cervical cancer; therefore, routine morphology alone was still insufficient to further determine the tumor origin and subtype. The purpose of immunohistochemistry is to differentiate primary lung adenocarcinoma, a mucinous adenocarcinoma phenotype, and metastatic carcinoma from other sites by integrating the patient's clinical features and pathologic morphology; meanwhile, Ki67 can reflect proliferative activity and help assess tumor biological behavior. In a patient like this case, who was initially misdiagnosed as having infection, had no endobronchial mass seen on bronchoscopy, and had diffuse lesions, immunohistochemistry helps increase the reliability of the pathologic diagnosis, reduce the risk of misclassifying primary lung cancer as metastatic carcinoma or an inflammatory lesion, and provide a basis for subsequent treatment decisions on whether to proceed according to a primary lung adenocarcinoma pathway.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Molecular pathology result: No mutations were detected in the sequences of exons 18, 19, 20, and 21 of the EGFR gene.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: In this case, needle biopsy pathology has already confirmed lung adenocarcinoma, but the patient is young, female, had an atypical infection-like onset, and has diffuse bilateral lung involvement, placing her among the patients with advanced lung adenocarcinoma in whom molecular subtyping must be completed as soon as possible. The core value of molecular pathology testing lies in identifying driver gene alterations and determining whether there is a molecular basis for targeted therapy, thereby directly influencing the choice of first-line treatment rather than remaining limited to empiric anti-infective therapy. In particular, this patient is critically ill, with progressively worsening dyspnea, an oxygenation index of less than 100, and a limited treatment window; if a sensitizing mutation is present, the treatment pathway and prognostic assessment could be markedly altered. Even if the results indicate no EGFR mutation, molecular pathology testing still accomplishes the evaluation of important therapeutic targets, helping exclude the possibility of EGFR-TKI treatment and supporting subsequent decision-making according to the treatment strategy for the mutation-negative population.

recommended_exams.exam: EGFR gene exon 18, 19, 20, and 21 sequence testing
recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: No mutations were detected in the sequences of EGFR exons 18, 19, 20, and 21.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient’s final pathology was lung adenocarcinoma, most likely primary, and the disease was already advanced with involvement of both lungs and mediastinal lymph nodes. For lung adenocarcinoma, EGFR exons 18, 19, 20, and 21 are among the most important and routinely tested sites related to targeted therapy. The purpose of testing is to determine whether the patient may benefit from EGFR-targeted drugs. In this case, given that the patient was a middle-aged woman, the pathologic type of lung adenocarcinoma was clearly established, the clinical progression was rapid, and the respiratory failure was severe, completing EGFR testing as soon as possible could directly answer the clinical question of whether there is an actionable precision-treatment entry point, which is very important for formulating a systemic treatment plan, avoiding blind medication use, and assessing prognosis. A result showing no mutation would help exclude indications for targeted therapy corresponding to common EGFR sensitizing mutations and suggest the need to shift to evaluation of other molecular markers or to treatment approaches such as non-EGFR-targeted therapy/chemotherapy.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text: CT-guided lung biopsy pathology result: (lung) well- to moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma, likely primary. Immunohistochemistry results: Napsin A (-), Ki67 (50%), TTF (-), MUC5AC (+), CA12-5 (-), EML-ALK (-), GATA3 (-); molecular pathology result: no mutations detected in EGFR exons 18, 19, 20, and 21.

treatment_plan: Treated with piperacillin/tazobactam, levofloxacin, imipenem/cilastatin sodium, combined with voriconazole antifungal therapy

Follow-up chest CT (Day 0): new cavitation is seen in some lesions, and the right lower lung lesion is larger than previously.
After anti-infective treatment, the patient still had dyspnea, cough with sputum production, and was unable to lie flat.
